textbook:
Clean cutaway textbook illustration of the CYTOSKELETON — the network of protein fibres inside a eukaryotic cell, NOT a bacterium and NOT a single organelle — shown as a wedge/corner of cytoplasm cut away near the plasma membrane, centred in a square 1:1 1080x1080 frame with generous negative space around the structures so labels can attach later. Fill the whole square edge-to-edge on a neutral dark-charcoal cytosol background with NO border, frame, vignette or letterbox. Match the exact house look of a refined educational plate: a MUTED, slightly desaturated palette (soft dusty tints, never bright primary or cartoon colours), THIN clean outlines (not heavy black strokes), gentle soft shading, each structure its own distinct soft colour fill.

THE THREE FIBRE TYPES MUST HAVE CLEARLY, OBVIOUSLY DIFFERENT THICKNESSES, in this exact order thinnest to thickest — this is the single most important requirement and a previous attempt got it WRONG (intermediate filaments must NEVER be as thick as or thicker than microtubules):
1. THINNEST: dusty coral-red MICROFILAMENTS — fine twisted two-strand beaded ropes, forming a dense mesh directly under a visible curve of plasma membrane at one edge (the cell cortex).
2. MEDIUM (clearly THINNER than the microtubules below — roughly HALF their tube diameter — only slightly thicker than the microfilaments): soft teal-green INTERMEDIATE FILAMENTS, a braided rope-like bundle crossing diagonally through the cytoplasm and anchoring at a small cell-junction patch at the membrane.
3. THICKEST BY FAR: steady mid-blue MICROTUBULES — unmistakably HOLLOW tubes, at least twice the diameter of the intermediate filaments. At least one microtubule must show a visible open circular bore/lumen at a cut end, and the tube surface should show a fine ridged lattice of parallel strands, never a smooth solid rod.

Have several microtubules radiate outward, star-like, from a small muted grey-brown hub (the CENTROSOME) positioned near a simplified rounded nucleus shape in one part of the frame.

MOTOR PROTEIN: on one microtubule, place a tiny warm amber-gold molecular motor — it must NOT be a human or humanoid figure: no head, no face, no arms, no human torso, no stick-figure body. Instead draw it as two small fused rounded globular domains (a tiny two-lobed blob, like a snowman-shaped molecule) with a few short curled leg-like appendages gripping the tube surface, towing a separate small pale round vesicle blob directly behind it as cargo.

CRITICAL SCIENTIFIC RULES: the three fibre types must never look the same thickness, and intermediate filaments must always read as clearly thinner than microtubules; microtubules are always hollow tubes, never solid rods; intermediate filaments have no directional arrows (no polarity); do not draw DNA, chromosomes or chromatin as fibres; do not draw a bacterial flagellum or any corkscrew propeller shape; the motor protein must never look like a person or stick figure; the whole composition should feel like an active construction site of ropes and rails, not a rigid static cage. Absolutely NO text, letters, numbers, labels, scale bars, arrows or watermarks in the image.
sem: Photorealistic false-color scanning electron micrograph view of the CYTOSKELETON of a eukaryotic cell after the plasma membrane and cytoplasm have been stripped away (an 'unroofed cell' preparation), revealing the bare meshwork of protein fibres beneath, centred in a square 1:1 1080x1080 frame filling the whole square edge-to-edge with NO border, frame or vignette. Crisp 3D surface texture, shallow depth of field, cool studio microscopy lighting, false-color palette: a dense mesh of very fine coral-red MICROFILAMENTS as the thinnest visible strands, medium-thickness teal-green braided INTERMEDIATE FILAMENTS clearly thicker than the microfilaments, and unmistakably thick, cylindrical mid-blue MICROTUBULES as the thickest fibres of all, several of them radiating outward across the frame from a denser knotted hub of fibre origins (the centrosome) toward the frame edges — at least one microtubule shown fractured or cut so its perfectly round HOLLOW BORE is visible, a true tube in cross-section, not a solid rod. Include one tiny two-legged amber-gold motor-protein particle gripping one of the microtubules, a small round vesicle-like blob attached behind it. Convey true relative scale — the size contrast between the three fibre thicknesses must be obvious at a glance. No text, no scale bar, no watermark. Looks like a real false-color SEM plate of exposed cytoskeletal filaments.
3d:
Stylized 3D medical-illustration still of the CYTOSKELETON inside a eukaryotic cell: soft global illumination, subsurface scattering on the translucent cytoplasm, clean seamless dark studio background filling the whole square 1:1 1080x1080 frame edge-to-edge with NO border, frame or vignette, gentle rim light, structures modeled with believable material but slightly idealized for clarity, scientific-animation look. Colorize with natural, believable biological tones so the three fibre types are clearly distinguishable and clearly, obviously DIFFERENT IN THICKNESS: fine, thin coral-red MICROFILAMENTS as a twisted two-strand rope mesh concentrated along one curved edge of translucent plasma membrane (the cell cortex); teal-green braided-rope INTERMEDIATE FILAMENTS clearly THINNER than the microtubules (roughly half their diameter) crossing the cytoplasm; and the clearly THICKEST fibres by far, steady mid-blue MICROTUBULES, rendered as genuinely HOLLOW tubes — light should pass through/reflect inside an open circular bore visible at any cut or broken end, with a subtly ridged surface of parallel strands, never a smooth solid rod. Several microtubules radiate outward in a star pattern from a compact grey-brown CENTROSOME hub positioned beside a simplified, softly glowing rounded nucleus shape.

MOTOR PROTEIN: along one microtubule, model a small warm amber-gold molecular motor — it must NOT be a human or humanoid figure and must have no head, no face, no arms, no human torso, no stick-figure body. Model it instead as two small fused rounded globular domains (a tiny two-lobed molecular blob) with a few short curled leg-like appendages gripping the tube surface, towing a separate small translucent pale vesicle sphere directly behind it as cargo.

Natural, believable biological tones throughout — not near-monochrome, not neon. No text, letters, numbers or watermarks anywhere. Single unified scene, not a diagram with callouts. The motor protein must never resemble a person.
watercolor:
Hand-painted watercolour naturalist plate of the CYTOSKELETON of a eukaryotic cell: soft washes, fine ink linework for outlines, aged-paper warmth, the composition of a 19th-century scientific atlas but anatomically modern and correct. The warm aged paper must FILL THE ENTIRE FRAME edge-to-edge and corner-to-corner — the paper IS the background, square 1:1 1080x1080. ZOOM IN CLOSE: the fibre bundle and the curved membrane arc must be painted LARGE, extending fully off all four edges of the square so no empty paper margin band remains anywhere — a previous attempt left too much bare paper around a small centred illustration; this time the composition must bleed off every edge, filling at least 92% of the frame with painted subject and its soft wash halo. No separate sheet/card/page lying on a table, no mat, no frame, no drop-shadow, no dark panel around a paper sheet.

Paint a wedge of cytoplasm near a curved stretch of plasma membrane, with rich translucent ink-and-wash strokes showing the three fibre types at CLEARLY, OBVIOUSLY DIFFERENT thicknesses (a previous attempt made them all look too similar):
1. THINNEST, finest strokes: dusty coral-red MICROFILAMENTS — a very fine, delicate twisted two-strand thread mesh hugging the membrane, painted with a light, thin brush line.
2. MEDIUM (clearly thicker than the microfilaments but still clearly THINNER than the microtubules — no more than half their width): teal-green braided ink strokes, the INTERMEDIATE FILAMENTS, crossing the cytoplasm like woven rope.
3. THICKEST, boldest strokes by far: mid-blue MICROTUBULES, painted as clearly HOLLOW tubes — at least one shown cut or broken to reveal a pale open bore down its centre, with fine parallel hatching along its length suggesting the ridged tubulin lattice, never a solid filled line.

Several microtubules radiate outward from a small muted brown centrosome hub near a simply-washed rounded nucleus shape.

MOTOR PROTEIN: along one microtubule, paint a tiny warm amber-gold molecular motor — it must NOT be a human or humanoid figure, no head, no face, no arms, no human torso, no stick-figure body. Paint it instead as two small fused rounded ink-and-wash blobs (a tiny two-lobed molecular shape) with a few short curled leg-like brush strokes gripping the tube, towing a small pale vesicle blob directly behind it on a fine ink thread.

Single specimen composition, no text, no letters, no scale bars, no watermark. Warm aged paper visible only as small slivers between fibres, never as a wide empty border.
